# Session 9: Iterative Prompt Improvement & Error Analysis

## 📋 Agenda

- Error analysis of misclassifications
- Iterate the prompt over 2–3 cycles
- A short under-the-hood walkthrough

## 🎯 Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

- Use `show_errors` to find misclassifications, hypothesize a fix, and re-run.
- Compare **macro-F1** across iteration rounds.
- Place your result next to the **published supervised results** for the same corpus — and say what that comparison does and does not license.
- Interpret what supervised training **buys and costs** versus zero-training prompting.

# Error analysis

## The number tells you *that*. The errors tell you *why*. {.smaller}

macro-F1 went from 0.31 to 0.34. **So what changed?**

. . .

You cannot answer that from the average. You have to look at what the model actually got wrong.

. . .

``` python
errors = show_errors(val, pred_cot)
errors.head(15)
```

Four columns: `id · gold · pred · text`.

## Read down the F1 column first

`evaluate` already printed per-class F1. One or two levels will sit far below the rest.

. . .

That is where macro-F1 is being lost — because it weights every class equally, **a collapsed rare class costs as much as a collapsed common one.**

. . .

Then read **three actual sentences** from that level. Counts locate the problem; only the sentences explain it.

## Two very different diagnoses {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note}
## "The model is wrong"
The sentence is clearly B1, the model said C1, and your scheme is unambiguous about it. → **a prompt problem**
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## "The scheme is fuzzy"
You and your partner would also disagree about this sentence. → **not fixable by prompting**
:::

. . .

Telling these apart is the single most valuable skill in your final report.

# Iterating the prompt

## The same move you already saw {.smaller}

Back in S7, **Huang & Mizumoto's Ex 1 → Ex 2** was a generic prompt tightened into a structured one.

. . .

That's exactly the loop here — only now it's **driven by data, not intuition**:

1. **read the errors** (`show_errors`) — where does the prompt fail?
2. **tighten one thing** — usually the *Criteria* / label descriptors.
3. **re-measure** macro-F1 — did it actually help?

::: {.callout-tip}
Change **one** thing per round, so you know *what* moved the number.
:::

## Say what you expect, before you run it {.smaller}

Three lines, filled in **before** you touch the prompt:

``` python
WORST_CLASS = "…"   # the level with the lowest F1
MY_CHANGE   = "…"   # the ONE thing you will change
I_PREDICT   = "…"   # what you expect, and why
```

. . .

This is what makes it a **study** rather than tinkering. A change that helps for a reason you named is a finding; one that helps for no reason you can give is a lucky guess.

. . .

Being wrong costs nothing. Being unable to say what you expected costs marks.

## Check the class you aimed at {.smaller}

Macro-F1 can **rise** while the level you targeted gets **worse** — another class quietly improved and carried the average.

. . .

So compare the F1 row for `WORST_CLASS`, before and after. Not the headline.

. . .

| # | Change | Why I expected it to help | macro-F1 | Target F1 | Right? |
|---|---|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 0 | *(no change)* | — | … | … | — |
| 1 | … | … | … | … | … |

Two logged rounds with reasons beat five undocumented ones.

# Under the hood

## What `run_prompt` has been doing {.smaller}

A read-only tour of the helper you have called all day — no editing, just so it is not a black box.

. . .

1. Drop each sentence into the `{text}` slot → one prompt per item.
2. Call the model, **paced** so you stay under 15 requests/minute.
3. On a `429`, wait and retry; on a *daily* quota error, stop immediately.
4. Scan the reply for the first CEFR level and keep it.
5. Return a plain list of labels, in gold order.

. . .

Step 4 is the fragile one — and it is why the CoT prompt forbids mentioning other levels.

# The LLM is one option, not the only one

## How good is 0.36, really? {.smaller}

Arase, Uchida & Kajiwara (2022) — the paper behind this corpus — trained models on **this exact task** (their Table 6):

| System | macro-F1 | weighted κ |
|---|:--:|:--:|
| Bag-of-words + SVM | 41.2 | 0.354 |
| *k*-NN over frozen BERT | 38.8 | 0.373 |
| BERT-Base, loss-weighted | 82.5 | 0.609 |
| Their proposed model | **84.5** | **0.628** |
| *Our zero-shot prompt (72 items)* | *≈36* | *0.849* |

## Two uncomfortable readings {.smaller}

**1. Zero-shot prompting lands near bag-of-words — not near BERT.**

The gap to 84.5 is what a labelled training set buys. CEFR-SP took trained experts to build. That is the cost side of the trade.

. . .

**2. Our weighted κ looks *better* than theirs. It is not.**

. . .

Their test set is 3,012 sentences with the natural imbalance; ours is a balanced 72. **κ is sensitive to the marginals.**

. . .

A number that flatters you across two different test sets is exactly the comparison a reader should refuse — and the one your report must not make.

## What this licenses {.smaller}

::: {.callout-important}
"The model got 0.36" means nothing until you can say **0.36 compared to what, on which items**.
:::

. . .

Claimable: *"a zero-shot prompt reaches roughly bag-of-words performance on this task"*.

. . .

Not claimable: *"our prompt beat the published model on agreement"*.

## Assistant, not replacement {.smaller}

Neither approach is "the answer" — each has costs: data to train vs. a prompt to write, reproducibility, interpretability.

. . .

And back to where the running example started — Huang & Mizumoto (2025):

> *"Human teachers must ultimately remain at the core of language teaching and learning."*

The LLM is a tool you **evaluate and supervise**, not a verdict you accept.
